clinicalPearls: A benign renal epithelial tumour arising from the intercalated cells of the collecting duct
Usually discovered incidentally as a well-defined solid cortical mass
May show a central stellate scar on imaging, though this is neither sensitive nor specific
Cannot be reliably distinguished from chromophobe renal cell carcinoma by imaging alone
Renal mass biopsy can suggest the diagnosis but sampling and hybrid oncocytic tumours limit certainty
Multiple oncocytomas or oncocytosis may occur in Birt-Hogg-Dube syndrome
Because malignancy cannot always be excluded preoperatively, many lesions are still resected
reference.pathophysiology: Renal oncocytoma is composed of oncocytes, cells packed with mitochondria that give an eosinophilic granular cytoplasm, and is thought to derive from the intercalated cells of the collecting duct. It is a benign neoplasm without metastatic potential, but it shares histological and immunophenotypic features with chromophobe renal cell carcinoma, which complicates diagnosis. Hybrid oncocytic-chromophobe tumours occur, particularly in the setting of Birt-Hogg-Dube syndrome, reflecting overlap in their cell of origin.
additionalDifferentials: Clear cell renal cell carcinoma with eosinophilic features
Papillary renal cell carcinoma, eosinophilic type
Hybrid oncocytic tumour in Birt-Hogg-Dube syndrome
additionalInvestigations: CT or MRI to characterise the solid renal mass
Renal mass biopsy where the result would change management
Immunohistochemistry to help separate it from chromophobe carcinoma
Assessment for Birt-Hogg-Dube features when tumours are multiple
Surveillance imaging when a conservative approach is chosen
redFlags: Interval growth or new symptoms suggesting the lesion is not benign
Multiple renal and cutaneous lesions suggesting a hereditary syndrome
Any histological atypia raising doubt about the benign diagnosis
reference.prognosis: Renal oncocytoma is benign with an excellent prognosis and does not metastasise; the main challenge is diagnostic certainty rather than tumour behaviour, and outcomes are excellent whether managed by surveillance or excision.
pitfalls: Relying on a central scar on imaging to diagnose it confidently
Assuming biopsy fully excludes chromophobe carcinoma
Over-treating a benign lesion or, conversely, under-treating a misclassified carcinoma
references: WHO Classification of Urinary and Male Genital Tumours
management: Offer active imaging surveillance for lesions confidently characterised as oncocytoma, as this benign tumour has no metastatic potential
Use renal mass biopsy with immunohistochemistry to support the diagnosis and separate it from chromophobe renal cell carcinoma where the result would change management
Proceed to nephron-sparing partial nephrectomy or excision when malignancy cannot be excluded, when hybrid oncocytic-chromophobe features are suspected, or when the lesion enlarges
Preserve renal function by favouring nephron-sparing over radical approaches given the benign nature of the tumour
Assess for Birt-Hogg-Dube syndrome when tumours are multiple or oncocytosis is present, examining for cutaneous and pulmonary features
Refer for genetic counselling and family screening if Birt-Hogg-Dube syndrome is confirmed
Continue surveillance imaging when a conservative approach is chosen to detect any change in size or characteristics
